analysis.one_liner: Repeals the entire Affordable Care Act, ending its coverage expansions, consumer protections, and taxes.
analysis.headline: The House passed full repeal of the Affordable Care Act 229–195 on May 16, 2013, with 227 Republicans in favor and 195 Democrats opposed, but the Senate never voted and the bill died at the end of the Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase the Affordable Care Act as if it had never passed, and erase the health care parts of the 2010 follow-up law, restoring the older rules [S2][S4]. That would end the insurance marketplaces and subsidies, the Medicaid expansion, protections for people with preexisting conditions, the ban on lifetime coverage limits, free preventive care, young adults staying on a parent's plan to 26, and the Medicare prescription-drug savings — and it would repeal the taxes that paid for those benefits, including a 3.8% tax on investment income that falls mostly on high earners [S2][S4]. The House passed it on a near-party-line vote, but the Democratic-run Senate never brought it to a vote before the Congress ended [S6][S8].
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households gain the most in cash: the bill repeals the ACA's 3.8% tax on investment income and the 0.9% extra Medicare tax on high wages, both of which fall on top earners [S2][S4]. Medical device makers and tanning businesses gain by shedding ACA excise taxes, and health insurers gain freedom from the rules that require them to cover preexisting conditions, spend premiums on medical care, and cap out-of-pocket burdens — though they also lose the subsidies and mandate that sent them millions of new customers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, medical device makers, health insurers

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the ACA and the health care provisions of the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010, restoring the law as it stood before 2010 [S2][S3][S4].

Removes the ACA's taxes, including the 3.8% net investment income tax and the additional Medicare tax on high earners found in the reconciliation act's health provisions, plus excise taxes on medical devices and indoor tanning [S2][S4].

Eliminates the individual mandate and the ACA's insurance regulations, including the requirement that insurers cover preexisting conditions and the medical loss ratio rules requiring them to spend premiums on care [S2][S4].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who gained from the ACA pay: the millions who bought subsidized marketplace coverage or gained Medicaid, the roughly 129 million people with preexisting conditions who would again face denials and exclusions, women losing free preventive screenings, young adults losing coverage on a parent's plan, and seniors paying more for prescriptions as the Medicare 'donut hole' closes. All of this is repealed without any replacement in the bill [S2][S4].
analysis.who_pays_short: Marketplace enrollees, people with preexisting conditions, seniors

drawbacks.text: Repeal strips coverage and protections from millions of people with no replacement in the bill: an amendment offered during debate to preserve protections for preexisting conditions, free preventive care, an end to lifetime limits, and coverage for young adults was rejected 190–230 [S6][S7].

Supporters' case: the ACA added new taxes, an individual mandate, and federal spending; repeal would restore the pre-2010 status quo and its budget outlook [S2]. The honest cost is that the bill removes benefits before proposing anything to replace them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains flow to concentrated interests — high-income households get tax cuts, device makers shed an excise tax, insurers shed regulation — while the costs fall broadly on people who had gained coverage, protections, and cheaper prescriptions. The bill offers nothing to replace what it takes away, so for ordinary people the trade is heavily one-sided.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it on a near-straight party-line vote, but the Senate put it on its calendar, never voted on it, and the bill died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Michele Bachmann introduced the bill on January 3, 2013, the first day of the new Congress, and 128 House Republicans — all Republicans — signed on as cosponsors [S1][S5].
On May 16, 2013, the Rules Committee set up debate under a rule closed to amendments, so no changes to the repeal were allowed [S6].

Rep. Lois Capps offered a motion to recommit — a last chance to send the bill back to committee — with instructions to preserve ACA benefits for women and children: free preventive screenings including breast cancer and gestational diabetes tests, coverage for preexisting conditions, the medical loss ratio rules, an end to lifetime benefit limits, and coverage for young adults up to age 26. It failed 190–230, with 226 of 232 Republicans voting no and 190 of 201 Democrats voting yes [S6][S7].
The House passed the repeal itself 229–195 later that day: 227 of 232 Republicans voted yes, 195 of 201 Democrats voted no [S8].

The Senate received the bill on May 20, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate calendar, where it sat. No committee considered it and no vote was ever scheduled; the Congress ended on January 3, 2015, with the repeal still on the calendar [S4][S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the Senate never acted, everyone covered or protected by the ACA kept those benefits through the Congress: the subsidized marketplace coverage, the Medicaid expansion, preexisting-condition protections, free preventive care, and lower Medicare drug costs. High-income households kept paying the ACA's investment income and Medicare taxes, and health insurers kept the subsidy revenue and the mandate customers that repeal would have taken away while leaving its regulations in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People who kept their ACA coverage and protections

for.name: Michele Bachmann
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the 113th Congress to repeal the ACA in its entirety.

for.name: 227 of 232 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on passage, and voted as a bloc against the motion to recommit that would have preserved preexisting-condition and preventive-care protections.

against.name: 195 of 201 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted no on passage, 190 of them also voting for the motion to recommit to preserve the ACA's benefits for women and children.

against.name: Lois Capps
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill with instructions to preserve preventive care for women, preexisting-condition coverage, medical loss ratio rules, an end to lifetime limits, and dependent coverage to age 26.

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the repeal to the Senate floor for a vote; the bill sat on the Senate calendar for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The vote was almost perfectly split by party: 227 of 232 Republicans voted for repeal and 195 of 201 Democrats voted against it; only 2 Democrats crossed over in favor.

industries.industry: High-income households and investment income earners
industries.note: The reconciliation act's health provisions included the 3.8% tax on net investment income and the 0.9% extra Medicare tax on high wages, both of which this bill repeals. Their gain is paid for by ending the coverage expansion and consumer protections those taxes financed [S2][S4].

Repeal frees insurers from preexisting-condition coverage requirements, the medical loss ratio rule, and other benefit mandates, but also ends the marketplace subsidies and the individual mandate that channeled millions of paying customers to them. The repeal would remove both the industry's obligations and its expanded customer base at the same time [S2][S4].
Full repeal wipes out the ACA's excise tax on medical devices, which helped finance the coverage expansion the device makers' customers rely on [S2][S4].
The ACA's 10% excise tax on indoor tanning services, part of the health provisions being repealed, would disappear; the tax was one of the revenue streams behind the ACA's benefits.
